claims.text: The untreated W–Cu composite develops phase separation and interfacial voids during processing and under relevant heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
Phase-separated regions and interfacial voids degrade the thermal conductivity of the untreated W–Cu composite.
Approximately 5 vol% Ni should be introduced during powder processing before densification.
Powder blending followed by spark plasma sintering can be used to incorporate the added material.
The processing route will distribute Ni uniformly at W/Cu interfaces.
Ni will form a stabilized Ni-rich interfacial layer between W and Cu.
The Ni-rich interfacial layer will reduce W/Cu interfacial energy.
Reduced interfacial energy will inhibit void nucleation and phase separation.
Ni acts as a sintering aid and wetting agent at W–Cu interfaces.
Ni increases mutual solubility at W–Cu boundaries.
Ni-mediated wetting and solubility reduce the driving force for phase separation and void formation during thermal treatment and irradiation.
Suppressing voids and phase separation maintains continuous, highly conductive W/Cu interfaces.
Under matched thermal cycling and irradiation, the Ni-modified composite will have less interfacial voiding and phase segregation than the untreated composite.
Under matched thermal cycling and irradiation, the Ni-modified composite will have higher thermal conductivity than the untreated composite.
Interfacial reactions and joint properties depend on processing temperature and time.
Moderate applied pressure during sintering can improve material properties.
Excessive diffusion or formation of unwanted secondary phases outside the proposed processing window may reduce the effectiveness of Ni.
The optimal Ni concentration and processing parameters are not yet established.
The long-term stability of a Ni-enriched W/Cu interface under extended irradiation is not established.
